prompt:
There are $n\ge3$ positive real numbers $a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n$. For each $1\le i\le n$ we let $b_i=\dfrac{a_{i-1}+a_{i+1}}{a_i}$ (here we define $a_0$ to be $a_n$ and $a_{n+1}$ to be $a_1$). Assume that for all $i$ and $j$ in the range $1$ to $n$, we have $a_i\le a_j$ if and only if $b_i\le b_j$.

Prove that $a_1=a_2=\cdots=a_n$.
answer: Proof: at a maximal $a_i$ we get $b_i\le2$, and this $b_i$ is the largest $b$, so all $b_j\le2$; but $\prod b_j\ge2^n$ by AM–GM. Hence all $b_j=2$, all $b_j$ are equal, and so all $a_j$ are equal.

solutions.title: Bound the largest b, then multiply
solutions.body:
Indices are taken modulo $n$.

**All $b_j\le2$.** Choose $i$ with $a_i$ maximal. Then $a_{i-1},a_{i+1}\le a_i$, so $b_i=\frac{a_{i-1}+a_{i+1}}{a_i}\le2$. For every $j$ we have $a_j\le a_i$, hence $b_j\le b_i\le2$ by the hypothesis.

**The product of the $b_j$ is at least $2^n$.** By AM–GM, $a_{j-1}+a_{j+1}\ge2\sqrt{a_{j-1}a_{j+1}}$, so
$$\prod_{j=1}^n b_j\ge\frac{2^n\prod_{j=1}^n\sqrt{a_{j-1}a_{j+1}}}{\prod_{j=1}^n a_j}=\frac{2^n\sqrt{\prod_j a_j\cdot\prod_j a_j}}{\prod_j a_j}=2^n ,$$
because each $a_k$ appears exactly twice under the square roots (as $a_{j-1}$ for $j=k+1$ and as $a_{j+1}$ for $j=k-1$).

**Conclusion.** All $b_j$ are positive and at most $2$, and their product is at least $2^n$, so $b_j=2$ for every $j$. Then for any $i,j$ we have both $b_i\le b_j$ and $b_j\le b_i$, so by the hypothesis $a_i\le a_j$ and $a_j\le a_i$, i.e. $a_i=a_j$. ∎

solutions.title: Neighbours of a maximum
solutions.body:
Let $a_i$ be minimal and $a_j$ maximal. Then
$$b_j=\frac{a_{j-1}+a_{j+1}}{a_j}\le2\le\frac{a_{i-1}+a_{i+1}}{a_i}=b_i ,$$
while $a_i\le a_j$ gives $b_i\le b_j$. So equality holds throughout, in particular $a_{j-1}+a_{j+1}=2a_j$ with $a_{j\pm1}\le a_j$, so $a_{j-1}=a_{j+1}=a_j$. Thus both neighbours of a maximal term are maximal. Walking around the cycle, every term is maximal, so all terms are equal. ∎

prompt:
We are given an acute triangle $ABC$. Let $D$ be the point on its circumcircle such that $AD$ is a diameter. Suppose that points $K$ and $L$ lie on segments $AB$ and $AC$, respectively, and that $DK$ and $DL$ are tangent to circle $AKL$.

Show that line $KL$ passes through the orthocentre of $ABC$.

*The orthocentre of a triangle is the point of intersection of its altitudes.*
answer: Proof: the midpoint $M$ of $KL$ is the orthocentre. $DM\perp KL$ and $DB\perp AB$ make $B,D,M,K$ concyclic, and the tangent–chord angle gives $\measuredangle(BM,AC)=90^\circ$; similarly $CM\perp AB$.

solutions.title: The midpoint of KL is the orthocentre
solutions.body:
We use directed angles $\measuredangle(\ell,m)$ between lines, modulo $180^\circ$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $KL$. We show $BM\perp AC$ and $CM\perp AB$, so $M$ is the orthocentre $H$; then $H=M$ lies on $KL$.

**Degenerate case $K=B$.** Then $DB$ is tangent to circle $AKL$ at $B$, and $DB\perp AB$ (as $AD$ is a diameter), so $AB$ is a diameter of circle $AKL$. Hence $\angle ALB=90^\circ$, so $BL$ is the altitude from $B$, and the line $KL=BL$ contains $H$. The case $L=C$ is the same. From now on $K\ne B$ and $L\ne C$.

**Concyclic points.** Tangent segments from $D$ are equal, $DK=DL$, so $DM\perp KL$. Since $AD$ is a diameter of the circumcircle, $DB\perp AB$, i.e. $\angle DBK=90^\circ$. So $B$ and $M$ both lie on the circle with diameter $DK$. Here $M\ne B$: otherwise $B$ would lie on line $KL$, and since $B,K$ lie on line $AB$, $L$ would lie on $AB$, forcing $L=A$. Also $M\ne D$, because $M$ lies inside circle $AKL$ and $D$ outside. Hence
$$\measuredangle(BM,BK)=\measuredangle(DM,DK).$$

**Angle chase.** By the tangent–chord theorem in circle $AKL$ (tangent $KD$ at $K$): $\measuredangle(KD,KL)=\measuredangle(AK,AL)=\measuredangle(AB,AC)$. Therefore
$$\measuredangle(DM,DK)=\measuredangle(DM,KL)+\measuredangle(KL,KD)=90^\circ-\measuredangle(AB,AC)=90^\circ+\measuredangle(AC,AB).$$
Since $BK$ is the line $AB$,
$$\measuredangle(BM,AC)=\measuredangle(BM,AB)+\measuredangle(AB,AC)=90^\circ+\measuredangle(AC,AB)+\measuredangle(AB,AC)=90^\circ .$$
So $BM\perp AC$, i.e. $M$ lies on the altitude from $B$. The same argument with the circle on diameter $DL$ (through $C$ and $M$) gives $CM\perp AB$.

Hence $M=H$, and the orthocentre is the midpoint of $KL$; in particular it lies on line $KL$. ∎

prompt:
Let $k$ be a positive integer. Lexi has a dictionary $\mathcal D$ consisting of some $k$-letter strings containing only the letters $A$ and $B$. Lexi would like to write either the letter $A$ or the letter $B$ in each cell of a $k\times k$ grid so that each column contains a string from $\mathcal D$ when read from top-to-bottom and each row contains a string from $\mathcal D$ when read from left-to-right.

What is the smallest integer $m$ such that if $\mathcal D$ contains at least $m$ different strings, then Lexi can fill her grid in this manner, no matter what strings are in $\mathcal D$?
answer: $m=2^{k-1}$. Strings ending in $B$ other than $BB\ldots B$ ($2^{k-1}-1$ of them) fail; with $2^{k-1}$ strings, either a constant string is present or two complementary strings $\ell,\ell'$ are, and the grid "$A$ iff row and column are on the same side of $J$" works, where $J$ is the set of $A$-positions of $\ell$.

solutions.title: A bad dictionary and complementary pairs
solutions.body:
**Answer: $m=2^{k-1}$.**

**$2^{k-1}-1$ strings are not enough.** Let $\mathcal D$ be all strings whose last letter is $B$, except the string $BB\ldots B$. It has $2^{k-1}-1$ strings. If Lexi filled the grid, every row would end in $B$, so the last column would read $BB\ldots B\notin\mathcal D$. So $m\ge2^{k-1}$. (For $k=1$ this dictionary is empty.)

**$2^{k-1}$ strings are enough.** Let $|\mathcal D|\ge2^{k-1}$.
- If $AA\ldots A\in\mathcal D$, fill every cell with $A$; similarly for $BB\ldots B$.
- Otherwise $\mathcal D$ consists of non-constant strings. Call two strings *complementary* if one is obtained from the other by swapping $A\leftrightarrow B$ everywhere. The $2^k-2$ non-constant strings split into $2^{k-1}-1$ complementary pairs. Since $|\mathcal D|\ge2^{k-1}$, by pigeonhole $\mathcal D$ contains both strings $\ell,\ell'$ of some pair.

Let $J\subseteq\{1,\dots,k\}$ be the set of positions where $\ell$ has an $A$ (so $\ell'$ has $B$ exactly there). Write $A$ in cell (row $r$, column $c$) if $r$ and $c$ are both in $J$ or both outside $J$, and $B$ otherwise.
- Row $r$ with $r\in J$: position $c$ holds $A$ exactly when $c\in J$, so the row reads $\ell$.
- Row $r$ with $r\notin J$: position $c$ holds $A$ exactly when $c\notin J$, so the row reads $\ell'$.
- The rule is symmetric in $r$ and $c$, so the columns read $\ell$ or $\ell'$ in the same way.

All rows and columns are in $\mathcal D$. Hence the smallest such $m$ is $2^{k-1}$. ∎

prompt:
Turbo the snail sits on a point on a circle with circumference $1$. Given an infinite sequence of positive real numbers $c_1,c_2,c_3,\ldots$, Turbo successively crawls distances $c_1,c_2,c_3,\ldots$ around the circle, each time choosing to crawl either clockwise or counterclockwise.

For example, if the sequence $c_1,c_2,c_3,\ldots$ is $0.4,0.6,0.3,\ldots$, then Turbo may start crawling as shown in the picture.

Determine the largest constant $C>0$ with the following property: for every sequence of positive real numbers $c_1,c_2,c_3,\ldots$ with $c_i<C$ for all $i$, Turbo can (after studying the sequence) ensure that there is some point on the circle that it will never visit or crawl across.

solutions.title: Always take the longer arc; alternating sequence for C > 1/2
solutions.body:
**Answer: $C=\frac12$.**

**$C=\frac12$ works.** Let all $c_i<\frac12$. Turbo fixes a point $P$ different from its starting point. Whenever Turbo is at a point $X\ne P$, the two arcs from $X$ to $P$ have total length $1$, so one of them has length at least $\frac12>c_i$. Turbo crawls in the direction of that arc. It stops before reaching $P$, so it never visits or crosses $P$, and it is again at a point different from $P$. By induction Turbo avoids $P$ forever. (Any $C<\frac12$ works as well, so the largest constant is at least $\frac12$.)

**No $C>\frac12$ works.** Write $C=\frac12+a$ with $a>0$ and take the sequence
$$\tfrac12,\ \tfrac{1+a}2,\ \tfrac12,\ \tfrac{1+a}2,\ \dots,$$
all of whose terms are less than $C$. Note that two consecutive terms add up to $1+\frac a2>1$.
- If Turbo ever crawls in the same direction twice in a row, it crawls a continuous stretch of length more than $1$ in one direction, so it passes over every point.
- Otherwise Turbo alternates directions. Lift the motion to the real line (the circle is $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$), starting at $0$, and say the first move is in direction $\varepsilon=\pm1$. Each pair of moves changes the position by $\varepsilon\cdot\frac12-\varepsilon\cdot\frac{1+a}2=-\varepsilon\frac a2$. Choose $N$ with $N\frac a2>1$. After $2N$ moves the lifted position is $-\varepsilon N\frac a2$, at distance more than $1$ from $0$. The lifted path is continuous, so it covers an interval of length more than $1$, whose image is the whole circle.

In both cases Turbo visits or crosses every point. So the property fails for every $C>\frac12$, and the answer is $C=\frac12$. ∎

prompt:
We are given a positive integer $s\ge2$. For each positive integer $k$, we define its *twist* $k'$ as follows: write $k$ as $as+b$, where $a,b$ are non-negative integers and $b<s$, then $k'=bs+a$. For the positive integer $n$, consider the infinite sequence $d_1,d_2,\ldots$ where $d_1=n$ and $d_{i+1}$ is the twist of $d_i$ for each positive integer $i$.

Prove that this sequence contains $1$ if and only if the remainder when $n$ is divided by $s^2-1$ is either $1$ or $s$.
answer: Proof: $k'\equiv sk\pmod{s^2-1}$, so $d_{i+2}\equiv d_i$; the twist strictly decreases numbers $\ge s^2$ and is an involution below $s^2$. So the sequence ends in a 2-cycle below $s^2$ whose residues are those of $d_1,d_2$; it is $\{1,s\}$ iff $n\equiv1$ or $s$.

solutions.title: Residues are 2-periodic, values eventually 2-periodic
solutions.body:
Write $k=as+b$ with $0\le b<s$, so $k'=bs+a$. Since $k\ge1$, also $k'\ge1$.

**Fact 1.** $k'\equiv sk\pmod{s^2-1}$. Indeed $sk-k'=as^2+bs-bs-a=a(s^2-1)$. Consequently $k''\equiv sk'\equiv s^2k\equiv k$, so
$$d_{i+2}\equiv d_i\pmod{s^2-1}\quad\text{for all }i,\qquad d_2\equiv s\,d_1 .$$

**Fact 2.** If $k\ge s^2$, then $k'<k$. From $as+b\ge s^2$ and $b\le s-1$ we get $a\ge s$. Then
$$k'=bs+a\le(s-1)s+a\le(s-1)a+a=as\le k .$$
Equality throughout would need $b=s-1$ and $b=0$, impossible as $s\ge2$. So $k'<k$.

**Fact 3.** If $k<s^2$, then $k'<s^2$ and $k''=k$. Here $0\le a,b\le s-1$, so $k'=bs+a\le s^2-1$, and the twist of $bs+a$ is $as+b=k$.

By Fact 2 the sequence strictly decreases while its terms are $\ge s^2$, so some term $d_j$ is $<s^2$. By Fact 3, from then on the sequence alternates $d_j,d_{j+1},d_j,d_{j+1},\dots$ with both values in $[1,s^2-1]$.

**($\Rightarrow$)** Suppose $d_i=1$. Then $d_{i+1}=1'=s$ (as $1=0\cdot s+1$). By Fact 1, $d_1$ is congruent to $d_i$ or $d_{i+1}$ (according to the parity of $i$), so $n\equiv1$ or $n\equiv s\pmod{s^2-1}$.

**($\Leftarrow$)** Suppose $n\equiv1$ or $s$. Since $s\cdot1=s$ and $s\cdot s\equiv1$, Fact 1 gives $\{d_1,d_2\}\equiv\{1,s\}$ modulo $s^2-1$. By Fact 1 again, the two values $d_j,d_{j+1}$ of the final cycle are congruent to $d_1,d_2$ in some order. So one of them is congruent to $1$. The only integer in $[1,s^2-1]$ that is $\equiv1\pmod{s^2-1}$ is $1$ itself. Hence the sequence contains $1$. ∎

prompt:
Let $ABC$ be a triangle with circumcircle $\Omega$. Let $S_b$ and $S_c$ respectively denote the midpoints of the arcs $AC$ and $AB$ that do not contain the third vertex. Let $N_a$ denote the midpoint of arc $BAC$ (the arc $BC$ containing $A$). Let $I$ be the incentre of $ABC$. Let $\omega_b$ be the circle that is tangent to $AB$ and internally tangent to $\Omega$ at $S_b$, and let $\omega_c$ be the circle that is tangent to $AC$ and internally tangent to $\Omega$ at $S_c$. Show that the line $IN_a$, and the line through the intersections of $\omega_b$ and $\omega_c$, meet on $\Omega$.

*The incentre of a triangle is the centre of its incircle, the circle inside the triangle that is tangent to all three sides.*
answer: Proof: the radical axis of $\omega_b,\omega_c$ is $AT$, where $T$ is the intersection of the tangents to $\Omega$ at $S_b,S_c$ (use $AP_b=AP_c$ for the tangency points on $S_bS_c$). The midpoint $M$ of $S_bS_c$ is the midpoint of $IN_a$, and the second intersection $X$ of $AT$ with $\Omega$ satisfies $O,M,A,X$ concyclic, which gives $X\in MN_a$.

solutions.title: Radical axis AT, then the midpoint of S_bS_c
solutions.body:
Let $O$ be the centre of $\Omega$ and $S_a$ the midpoint of arc $BC$ not containing $A$. Recall the *incentre–excentre lemma*: $S_bA=S_bI$ and $S_cA=S_cI$. So **$S_bS_c$ is the perpendicular bisector of $AI$**.

**Part I: the radical axis of $\omega_b$ and $\omega_c$ is $AT$.**

Arc $S_cAS_b$ measures $\angle C+\angle B<180^\circ$, so $S_bS_c$ is not a diameter and the tangents to $\Omega$ at $S_b$, $S_c$ meet at a point $T$, with $TS_b=TS_c$.
- *The point $T$.* The tangent to $\Omega$ at $S_b$ is also tangent to $\omega_b$ (the circles touch there), so $\operatorname{pow}_{\omega_b}(T)=TS_b^2=TS_c^2=\operatorname{pow}_{\omega_c}(T)$.
- *The point $A$.* Let $\omega_b$ touch $AB$ at $P_b$. The homothety with centre $S_b$ and positive ratio taking $\omega_b$ to $\Omega$ maps line $AB$ to a parallel line tangent to $\Omega$, at a point $P_b^*$ on ray $S_bP_b$ beyond $P_b$. So $P_b^*$ is the midpoint of the arc $AB$ on the other side of $AB$ from $S_b$. As $S_b$ lies on the arc $ACB$, this is the arc not containing $C$, so $P_b^*=S_c$. Hence $P_b$ lies on $S_bS_c$, i.e. $P_b=AB\cap S_bS_c$. Similarly the tangency point $P_c$ of $\omega_c$ with $AC$ is $AC\cap S_bS_c$. The line $S_bS_c$ is perpendicular to the bisector $AI$ of $\angle P_bAP_c$, so triangle $AP_bP_c$ is isosceles: $AP_b=AP_c$. Thus $\operatorname{pow}_{\omega_b}(A)=AP_b^2=AP_c^2=\operatorname{pow}_{\omega_c}(A)$.

$T$ lies outside $\Omega$ and $A$ on it, so $T\ne A$. The line through the two intersection points of $\omega_b$ and $\omega_c$ is their radical axis, which is the line $AT$.

**Part II: $AT$ and $IN_a$ meet on $\Omega$.** If $AB=AC$ then $N_a=A$ lies on both lines and we are done; assume $AB\ne AC$, so $N_a\ne A$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $S_bS_c$. Since $TS_b=TS_c$ and $OS_b=OS_c$, the line $OT$ is the perpendicular bisector of $S_bS_c$ and passes through $M$; also $M\ne O$.

- *$M$ is the midpoint of $IN_a$.* $N_aS_a$ is a diameter, so $AN_a\perp AS_a=AI$. Together with $AI\perp S_bS_c$, this gives $AN_a\parallel S_bS_c$. So the line $OT$ ($\perp S_bS_c$, through $O$) is the perpendicular bisector of the chord $AN_a$, and $MA=MN_a$. Also $MA=MI$, as $M$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $AI$. So $M$ is the circumcentre of triangle $AIN_a$, which has a right angle at $A$. Hence $M$ is the midpoint of the hypotenuse $IN_a$; in particular $M\in IN_a$ and $M\ne N_a$.
- *$O,M,A,X$ are concyclic*, where $X$ is the second intersection of line $TA$ with $\Omega$. Note $TA$ is not tangent to $\Omega$ (the only tangency points from $T$ are $S_b,S_c$), so $X\ne A$. The power of $T$ gives $TA\cdot TX=TS_c^2$. In the right triangle $TS_cO$ (right angle at $S_c$), $M$ is the foot of the altitude from $S_c$, so $TS_c^2=TM\cdot TO$. Hence $TA\cdot TX=TM\cdot TO$. The points $A,X$ are not on line $OT$: $A\in OT$ would give $A=N_a$. So by the converse of the power of a point, $O,M,A,X$ are concyclic.
- *$X$ lies on $MN_a$.* If $X=N_a$ there is nothing to show. Otherwise, with directed angles modulo $180^\circ$, concyclicity gives $\measuredangle(XA,XM)=\measuredangle(OA,OM)$. Let $t$ be the tangent to $\Omega$ at $A$. By the tangent–chord theorem, $\measuredangle(XA,XN_a)=\measuredangle(t,AN_a)$. Since $t\perp OA$ and $AN_a\perp OM$, rotating both lines by $90^\circ$ gives $\measuredangle(t,AN_a)=\measuredangle(OA,OM)$. Hence $\measuredangle(XA,XN_a)=\measuredangle(XA,XM)$, so $X$, $M$, $N_a$ are collinear.

So $X$ lies on line $MN_a=IN_a$ and on line $AT$, the radical axis of $\omega_b$ and $\omega_c$. Since $X\in\Omega$, the two lines meet on $\Omega$. ∎
